prerequisites.title: X account and Developer Agreement
prerequisites.detail: Sign in to console.x.com with an X account, accept the Developer Agreement and Policy, and describe how you will use the API.

prerequisites.title: Prepaid credits
prerequisites.detail: Buy credits in the Developer Console before making API requests; they are deducted per use.

prerequisites.title: X representative
prerequisites.detail: Ads API Standard Access and token-limit increases go through your X representative.

steps.title: Sign in and accept the agreement
steps.detail: Sign in at console.x.com, accept the Developer Agreement and Policy, and fill in the usage profile.
steps.done_when: You can reach the Developer Console dashboard.

steps.title: Create the app
steps.detail: Click New App and enter the name, description and use case.
steps.done_when: The console shows your new app.

steps.title: Draft app description and use case
steps.detail: An agent can write the name, description and use case text, requesting only needed scopes.

steps.title: Save the client ID and secret
steps.detail: Copy credentials immediately; they are shown only once and regenerating invalidates the old ones.
steps.done_when: Client ID and secret are stored securely.

steps.title: Create the Composio auth config
steps.detail: Create a custom auth config with your client ID and secret. Copy the redirect URI from the Composio dashboard.

steps.title: Register callback URL in the X app
steps.detail: Add the Composio redirect URI to the app's settings on developer.x.com, since X requires callbacks to be configured there.
steps.done_when: Callback URL is saved in app settings.

steps.title: Buy credits
steps.detail: Purchase credits in the Developer Console; auto-recharge needs a saved default payment method.

steps.title: Contact your X representative
steps.detail: Ask to apply for Standard Access for the extra Ads API endpoints.

traps.title: Rate limits are set per app for Bearer Token
traps.detail: Rate limits are set per app for Bearer Token (app-only) requests and per user for OAuth 1.0a or OAuth 2.0 user tokens; the page does not say these limits differ for unreviewed apps.

traps.title: Credentials are shown only once
traps.detail: If lost, you must regenerate them, which invalidates the old ones and can break connected setups.

traps.title: Token cap on older Ads API apps
traps.detail: Apps that requested Ads API access before July 2023 may be limited to 5 user OAuth tokens. Raising it requires your X representative.

traps.title: Costs run separately from rate limits
traps.detail: You can stay within rate limits and still be charged, and hitting a limit returns a 429 error.

traps.title: Pay-per-usage read cap
traps.detail: Pay-per-usage plans cap at 3 million Post reads per monthly cycle; more needs an Enterprise plan.

traps.title: Old developer-account reviews were slow
traps.detail: Community posts from 2020-2021 report waits from a couple of days to over a month, with rejections lacking reasons. These may not reflect the current process.

blockers.what_it_means: You exceeded the endpoint's rate limit for the window.
blockers.what_to_do: Wait for the window to reset and reduce request volume.
blockers.agent_can_help: Add retry with backoff to the agent's calls.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: "Composio wants to access your account" on Google, GitHub, etc.
evidence.answer: With Composio's default setup, the provider's OAuth consent screen shows the text "Composio wants to access your account" on Google, GitHub, etc.; using your own OAuth app is the stated fix.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Add your own OAuth app only for toolkits where the provider consent screen must show your brand.
evidence.answer: You should add your own OAuth app only for toolkits where the provider consent screen must show your brand.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: In your OAuth app's settings, set the authorized redirect URI to your own endpoint:
evidence.answer: The page's proxy setup registers your own domain's endpoint as the authorized redirect URI in your OAuth app, which then forwards to Composio's callback.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Composio registers and maintains OAuth apps for popular toolkits such as GitHub, Gmail, and Slack. You do not need to register your own OAuth app.
evidence.answer: Composio registers and maintains its own OAuth apps for popular toolkits such as GitHub, Gmail, and Slack, so the developer does not need to register their own.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: You provide your own OAuth app, API key, bearer token, or other credentials and tell Composio to use them for a toolkit.
evidence.answer: With a custom auth config, the developer supplies their own OAuth app (or API key, bearer token, or other credentials) and tells Composio to use them for a toolkit.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Managed apps are the default when they are available.
evidence.answer: Managed apps are the default when they are available.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: To check whether Composio provides the OAuth app for a toolkit, see [Managed OAuth apps](/toolkits/managed-auth).
evidence.answer: To check whether Composio provides the OAuth app for a given toolkit, the page points to the Managed OAuth apps page.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Users will see "Composio wants to access your account" during OAuth.
evidence.answer: During OAuth with a managed app, users see a Composio-branded consent message rather than the developer's app name.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: In production, users should see your app name, not "Composio." This is the most common reason to switch.
evidence.answer: Managed apps are a good fit for internal tools, prototypes, and development, but in production users should see the developer's app name instead of Composio.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Composio's default scopes may not include everything you need (e.g., write access to a specific Google API).
evidence.answer: Managed apps use Composio's default scopes, which may not include everything needed; custom scopes (for example write access to a specific Google API) require the developer's own app.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Managed apps share quota across all Composio users. Your own app gets a dedicated quota.
evidence.answer: Limit of the managed app: managed apps share quota across all Composio users, whereas the developer's own app gets a dedicated quota.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Managed auth enforces a 15-minute minimum polling interval; your own app can use shorter polling intervals where supported.
evidence.answer: Limit of the managed app: managed auth enforces a 15-minute minimum polling interval for triggers, while the developer's own app can use shorter polling intervals where supported.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Self-hosted or regional variants (e.g., a private Salesforce subdomain) need their own OAuth app.
evidence.answer: Self-hosted or regional variants of an app, such as a private Salesforce subdomain, need their own OAuth app rather than the managed one.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Enterprise customers require your branding end-to-end.
evidence.answer: Enterprise customers who require the developer's branding end-to-end call for a custom app rather than the managed one.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Use your own credentials for toolkits where users see consent screens (GitHub, Google, Slack) and Composio managed auth for the rest.
evidence.answer: A developer can mix approaches: use their own credentials for toolkits where users see consent screens (e.g., GitHub, Google, Slack) and managed auth for the rest, with each toolkit getting its own auth config.

evidence.question: R1
evidence.quote: It usually takes a day or two, or sometimes more, for your application to be reviewed by Twitter.
evidence.answer: Developer-written guide (2021, community blog, not official) reports that developer-account application review usually took a day or two, sometimes longer.

evidence.question: R1
evidence.quote: Twitter doesn't specify why they rejected an application.
evidence.answer: Rejections were reported without a stated reason; the same guide notes that policy-violation cases can instead get a review email asking the applicant to amend the application and reply to it.

evidence.question: R1
evidence.quote: アプリの申込み（申請）から1か月以上たって、ようやく審査結果が来ました。結果は不合格です。
evidence.answer: A 2020 Japanese blog reports about a one-month wait from application to result (applied 12 Apr 2020, result 14 May 2020, during COVID delays), ending in rejection with a reason the applicant said they never received a request for.
